Several scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. beatiludinem, sancio, eigo, transgressores for transgressor es). The Isaiah quotation's phrase 'better than sons and daughters' renders 'meliorem a filiis et filiabus'. The citation 'Matth. vii, 11' in section 5 should be Matt. 7:12; 'Ps. xxxiii, 15' follows Vulgate numbering (Ps. 34:14 in English Bibles).

§7: 'propter innocentiae voluntatem' is odd; one might expect 'incontinentiae' (i.e. those who use the apostolic remedy of marriage because of incontinence, 1 Cor. 7:9); translated as printed. 'abutuntur' taken in its neutral sense 'make use of'. §8: the quotation 'Quaecunque sunt sancta...' is Phil. 4:8, not Ps. 4:8 as the edition cites. §9: 'Manus ne porrectae ad accipiendum sint, ad dandum autem collectae' literally says the hands should be 'drawn in for giving', which inverts the sense of Ecclus. 4:31 (open to receive, closed to give); the text may be corrupt, likely intending the reverse; translated literally. The 'Make a straight path' citation is closer to Heb. 12:13 / Prov. 4:26 than Isa. 57:14; the citation for Prov. 3:3 is printed as iii, 15. 'quoniam auditu et visu justus erat' refers to Lot (2 Pet. 2:8). Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'sanctiacationem', 'urgata' for purgata, 'documema').

The scripture references are given as the edition prints them, though some are inexact (e.g. Matt. 5:17 for 5:28; Rev. "ibid. 4, 5" for 14:5). "Diligit Dominus sancta corda..." is quoted without a reference; it echoes Prov. 22:11 (Vulgate). In §12, "lamentis" (laments) may be a scanning error for "lomentis" (cleansing washes), which would suit "nitro" better. In §11, "in incorruptibilitate qu(??)" is taken as "quieti".

Biblical references printed in the edition are sometimes wrong; corrected in translation where evident: Jer. 48:10 (printed xlvi), Luke 2:52 (printed II, 25), Matt. 10:22 (printed xxii), Isa. 66:2 (printed lxvi, 3); 'Ps. 74:5' is misplaced (the allusion is to Ps. 14:4). 'Auge eis mala...' is Isa. 26:15 (Old Latin). In §17 'Salis' read as 'Satis'. In §16 'ut tunc, si forte loquaris, quando tacere peccatum sit' is awkward; rendered literally.

nodes.text: EXHORTATION TO A BRIDE OF CHRIST.

1. How great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heaven we are taught, besides the testimonies of the Scriptures, by the custom of the Church as well: for we learn that a special merit belongs to that which has a special consecration. For while the whole crowd of believers receives equal gifts of grace, and all glory in the same blessings of the sacraments, these [virgins] have something of their own beyond the rest, since out of that holy and spotless flock of the Church they are chosen by the Holy Spirit, as holier and purer victims, for the merits of their will, and are offered on the altar of God by the high priest. Truly a victim worthy of the Lord is the offering of so precious a living creature, and no victim will please him more than one in his own image. For it is of such, I think, that the Apostle chiefly spoke: "I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God" (Rom. 12:1). Virginity therefore possesses both what others have and what others do not have: for it holds both the common and a special grace, and rejoices in its own privilege, so to speak, of consecration. For the authority of the Church also allows us to call virgins brides of Christ, since it veils those whom it consecrates to the Lord after the manner of brides, showing that those will most of all have a spiritual marriage who have escaped carnal union. And worthily are they joined spiritually to God by the likeness of marriage, who for love of him have spurned human marriages. In them above all is fulfilled that saying of the Apostle: "But he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit" (1 Cor. 6:17).

2. It is a great and immortal thing, almost beyond bodily nature, to lull lust to sleep, to quench by strength of mind the flame of desire kindled by the torches of youth, to shut out by spiritual effort the force of natural pleasure, to live against the custom of the human race, to despise the comforts of a spouse, to scorn the sweetness of children, and to count as nothing, in hope of future blessedness, whatever can be the advantages of the present life. This, as I said, is a great and admirable virtue, and not undeservedly destined for a vast reward in proportion to the greatness of its toil. "I will give," says the Lord, "to my eunuchs in my house and within my wall a named place better than sons and daughters of Israel; I will give them an everlasting name that will not fail" (Isa. 56:4). Of these eunuchs the Lord speaks again in the Gospel, saying: "For there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" (Matt. 19:12). Great indeed is the toil of chastity, but greater the reward: the guarding is temporal, but the recompense eternal. Of these too the blessed apostle John speaks, that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14:4). Think this is to be understood thus: that no place in the heavenly court is to be closed to them, and all the dwellings of the divine mansions are to be opened to them. But that the merit of virginity may shine more brightly, and how worthy of God it is may be understood more plainly, let this be considered: that our Lord and Saviour God, when for the salvation of the human race he deigned to take on man, chose no other than a virginal womb. And to show that such a thing pleased him very greatly, and to commend the good of chastity to both sexes, he, who would remain a virgin, had a virgin mother; in himself to men, and in his mother to women, he offered an example of virginity, by which it might be shown that in both sexes blessed integrity is held to belong to the divinity and to have deserved its fullness, since whatever was found in the son was wholly in the mother. But why do I busy myself to reveal the excellent and sublime merit of chastity and to display the good of glorious virginity, when I know well that many have spoken at length on this matter and proved its blessedness by the clearest reasons, and that no wise person can doubt that a thing which involves greater toil is of greater merit? For whoever reckons chastity worthy of no reward, or a small one, it is certain that he either does not know it or bears its toil unwillingly. Hence those always disparage chastity who either do not have it or are forced to have it against their will.

3. Now therefore, since we have shown, though briefly, both the toil and the merit of integrity, we must keep watch more carefully, lest a thing which consists in great virtue and is destined for a vast reward should be deprived of its fruit. For the more precious any kind of thing is, the greater the care with which it is guarded. And since there are many things which lose their own good unless they are helped by the aid of other things, as is the case with honey, which, unless it is preserved, and (to speak more truly) nourished, by the protection of wax and the cells of the honeycomb, loses its natural charm and cannot subsist by itself. So also with wine, which, unless the vessel is of good smell and is kept with pitch frequently renewed, loses the force of its natural sweetness. We must therefore take care more attentively lest perhaps virginity too needs other things, without which it can by no means bear fruit, and so great a toil profit nothing, while that is vainly believed to profit which is possessed without the necessary things. For unless I am mistaken, the integrity of chastity is kept for the reward of the heavenly kingdom, which, it is certain enough, no one can attain without the merit of eternal life. And Scripture testifies that eternal life can be earned only by keeping all the divine commandments, saying: "If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments" (Matt. 19:17). So no one has life except one who has kept all the commandments of the law; and one who does not have life cannot possess the heavenly kingdom, in which not the dead but the living will reign. Virginity alone, then, which hopes for the glory of the heavenly kingdom, will profit nothing unless it also has that to which perpetual life is promised, through which the reward of the heavenly kingdom is possessed. Before all things, therefore, those who keep chastity and integrity and hope for its recompense from God's justice must keep the precepts of the commandments, lest the toil of glorious chastity and continence be brought to nothing. That virginity is above commandment or precept, no one who is wise and reads is unaware, since the Apostle says: "Concerning virgins I have no precept of the Lord, but I give counsel" (1 Cor. 7:25). Since, then, he gives counsel for keeping virginity and does not lay down a precept, he has declared it to be above commandment or precept. Whoever, then, keep virginity, do more than is commanded. For to have done more than was ordered will profit only if you do what was ordered. Desiring to fulfil the divine counsel, keep the commandment before all things; wishing to obtain the reward of virginity, embrace the merits of life, so that your chastity can be rewarded. For as the recompense of the commandments bestows life, so on the contrary their transgression brings forth death. And one who through transgression has been assigned to death cannot hope for the crown of virginity, nor, being placed in punishment, expect the reward of chastity.

4. For there are three kinds [of virtue] through which entry is made into possession of the heavenly kingdom. The first is chastity; the second, contempt of the world; the third, justice. As these, when joined, greatly benefit those who possess them, so when divided they can hardly profit, since each of them is demanded not for its own sake only but for the sake of another. First, then, chastity is sought, so that contempt of the world may follow more easily: for the world can more lightly be despised by those who are not held by the bonds of marriage. And contempt of the world is required so that justice may be kept, which those can hardly fulfil who are entangled in the business of worldly goods and earthly pleasures. Whoever, therefore, possesses the first kind, chastity, and does not obtain the second, which is contempt of the world, possesses the first almost to no purpose, since he lacks the second, for whose sake the first was sought. And if one has the first and second but lacks the third, which is justice, he labours in vain, since the two former are required chiefly for the sake of justice. For what does it profit to have chastity for the sake of contempt of the world, and not to have that for which you have it? Or why should you despise the things of the world if you do not keep justice, for whose sake it befits you to have chastity and contempt of the world? For as the first kind exists for the second, so the first and second exist for the third; and if that is absent, neither the first nor the second will profit.

5. Perhaps you say: then teach me what justice is, so that, once I know it, I may be able to fulfil it more easily. I will say briefly, as I can, and use the simplicity of ordinary words, because the matter we are treating is such that it ought by no means to be obscured by the more eloquent speech of fine rhetoric, but laid open by plainer narration: for a thing necessary to all ought to be shown in common speech. Justice, then, is nothing other than not sinning. And not sinning is keeping the precepts of the law. And the observance of the precepts is kept in two ways: that you do none of the things forbidden, and strive to fulfil all the things commanded. This is what it says: "Turn away from evil, and do good" (Ps. 33:15). For I do not want you to think that justice consists in this, that you do no evil, since not doing good is also evil, and in both the law is transgressed. For he who said, "Turn away from evil," also said, "do good." If you turn away from evil and do not do good, you are a transgressor of the Law, which is fulfilled not only in abhorring evil deeds but also in carrying out good works completely. For you are not commanded only not to strip the clothed of his garments, but also to cover the stripped with yours; nor only not to take away his own bread from one who has it, but to share yours gladly with one who has none; nor only not to drive the poor man from his own lodging, but to receive into yours one driven out and having none. For we are commanded "to weep with those who weep" (Rom. 12:15). How do we weep with them if we share in none of their needs, and give them no help in the things for which they weep? For God does not seek the fruitless moisture of our weeping; but since tears are a sign of grief, he wants you to feel another's distress as your own, and to help another as you would wish to be helped if you were in such trouble, because of that saying: "Whatever good things you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them" (Matt. 7:12). For to weep with one who weeps and, when you can, to give nothing to the one weeping is a sign of mockery, not of compassion. Indeed our Saviour wept with Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, and showed the feeling of his boundless mercy by the witness of tears; and works, the signs of true compassion, soon followed, when Lazarus, for whose sake the tears were shed, was raised and given back to his sisters. This was to weep with those who weep in true compassion: to take away the cause of weeping. "But he did it as one with power," you will say. Yet nothing impossible is commanded of you either: he has fulfilled everything who has done what he could.

6. But, as we had begun to say, it is not enough for a Christian to abstain from evil unless he also carries out the duties of good works. This is proved above all by that testimony in which the Lord threatens that those will be liable to eternal fire who, although they have done nothing evil, have not done all that is good, saying: "Then the King will say to those who are on the left: 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat,'" etc. (Matt. 25:41). He did not say: "Depart from me, you cursed, because you committed murder, or adultery, or thefts." For they are condemned and handed over to the punishments of eternal Gehenna not because they had done evil, but because they had not done good; not because they had committed what was forbidden, but because they refused to fulfil what was commanded. From this one must consider what hope those can have who still do some of the things that are forbidden, when even those who have not done what is commanded are guilty. For I do not want you to flatter yourself on this point, that if you have not done some things it is because you have done others, since it is written: "Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all" (Jas. 2:10). For Adam sinned once, and died; and do you think you live while often committing that which killed another when he had done it once? Or do you think he committed a great crime, for which he was rightly condemned to a harsher punishment? Let us see, then, what he did against the commandment. He ate of the fruit of a tree. What then? Did God punish man with death because of the fruit of a tree? Not because of the fruit of the tree, but because of contempt for the commandment. So the question is not of the nature of the sin, but of the transgression of the commandment. And he who told Adam not to eat of the fruit of the tree has himself commanded you not to curse, not to lie, not to disparage, not to listen to one who disparages, not to swear at all, not to covet, not to envy, not to be lukewarm, not to be avaricious; to repay no one evil for evil, to love your enemies, to bless those who curse you, to pray for those who slander and persecute you, to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes you, not to go to law in a worldly court, to let it go gladly if anyone wishes to take what is yours, not to admit the evil of anger, or jealousy, or spite within your breast, to flee the crime of avarice, to beware of every evil of pride and boasting, and to live humble and meek after the example of Christ, avoiding the company of the wicked so far that you do not even take food with fornicators, or the avaricious, or slanderers, or the envious, or detractors, or drunkards, or the rapacious. If you despise him in any of this, then if he spared Adam, he will spare you too. Indeed, Adam was rather the one to be spared, since he was still untaught and new, and was not held back by the example of anyone who had sinned before him and died because of his sin; but for you, after so many lessons, after the Law, after the Prophets, after the Gospels, after the Apostles, if you choose to do wrong, I do not know how he could pardon you.

7. Or do you flatter yourself on the privilege of virginity? Remember that Adam and Eve were virgins when they sinned, and that bodily integrity did not profit them as they sinned. A virgin who sins is to be compared to Eve, not to Mary. We do not deny that in the present time there is the remedy of penance; but we urge that one ought rather to hope for a reward than for pardon. For it is shameful for those who await the palm of virginity to ask for pardon of a fault, and for those who have castrated themselves even from lawful things to fall into something unlawful. For it is lawful to enter into the union of marriage. And just as those are to be praised who, for the love of Christ and the glory of the heavenly kingdom, have despised the bond of wedlock, so those are not to be condemned who, not yet vowed to God, make use of the apostolic remedy for the sake of [preserving] innocence. Therefore, as we have said, those who forsake marriage spurn not unlawful things but lawful ones. But if such women swear, if they curse, if they disparage, if they allow themselves to listen to those who disparage, if they repay evil for evil, if they incur the crime of greed for others' goods or of avarice with their own, if they harbour the poisons of jealousy or spite, if they say or think anything unseemly against the ordinances of the Law and the Apostles; if they go out adorned and decked in their zeal to please in the flesh; if they do any of the things which, as is usual, are unlawful, what will it profit them to have spurned what was lawful and to practise what is not lawful? If you wish the lawful thing you have despised to profit you, see that you do none of the things that are not lawful. For it is foolish to have feared what is less and not to fear what is greater, or not to avoid what is forbidden while shunning what is permitted. For the Apostle says: "The unmarried woman thinks of the things of the Lord, how she may please God, that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks of the things of this world, how she may please her husband" (1 Cor. 7:34). He declares that the married woman pleases her husband by thinking of the things of the world, but the unmarried woman pleases God, because she has no care for the world. Let her tell me, then, who has no husband and yet thinks of the things of the world: whom does she wish to please? Will not the married woman begin to be preferred to her? For the one, by thinking of the things of the world, at least pleases her husband; but this one can please neither a husband, whom she does not have, nor God.

8. But neither is it fitting for us to pass over in silence what he said: "The unmarried woman thinks of the things of the Lord, how she may please God, that she may be holy in body and spirit" (1 Cor. 7:34). What, then, are the things of the Lord? Let the Apostle say: "Whatever things are holy, whatever just, whatever lovely, whatever of good report; if there is any virtue, if any praise of discipline" (Phil. 4:8). These are the things of the Lord, which holy, true and apostolic virgins meditate on and think of day and night without any break in time. The kingdom of heaven is the Lord's; the resurrection of the dead is the Lord's; immortality is the Lord's; incorruption is the Lord's; the brightness of the sun which is promised to the saints is the Lord's, as is written in the Gospel: "Then the just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father" (Matt. 13:43). The many mansions of the saints in heaven are the Lord's; the thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold fruit is the Lord's. These things they think of, and they think by what works they may merit the things that are the Lord's. The law of the New and Old Testament is also the Lord's, in which the holy words of his mouth shine forth; if any virgins meditate on these without ceasing, they think of the things that are the Lord's, and in them is fulfilled that prophetic word: "Eternal foundations upon solid rock, and the commandments of the Lord in the heart of a holy woman" (Ecclus. 26:24). There follows: "how she may please God" — God, I say, not men — "that she may be holy in body and spirit" (1 Cor. 7:34). He did not say "that she may be holy in one member", or "in body" only, but "that she may be holy in body and spirit". For a member is one part of the body, while the body is the joining together of all the members. When, then, he says "that she may be holy in body", he testifies that she ought to be sanctified in all her members. For the sanctification of the other members will not profit if corruption is found even in one. And she who has been defiled by the pollution of even one [member] will no longer be holy in body, which consists of all the members.

9. But to make what I say plainer and clearer: suppose some woman is cleansed by the sanctification of all her members, and only her tongue sins, by blaspheming or bearing false witness; will all the members set the one free? Or will the rest also be judged because of the one? If, then, the sanctification of the other members will not profit when there is a fault in one, how much more will the integrity of one profit nothing if all are corrupted by the disgrace of various sins? Therefore I beg you, virgin, do not flatter yourself on chastity alone, nor trust in the integrity of one member; but, according to the Apostle, keep the holiness of the body for God alone. Cleanse your head of all defilement: for it is a crime, after its sanctification with the holy chrism, to soil it with the dye or powder of saffron or of any other pigment, or to adorn it with gold or gems of any earthly kind, since it already shines with the splendour of heavenly adornment. For to prefer worldly and secular ornament is a great insult to divine grace. Cleanse your forehead, so that it may blush at human, not divine works, and receive that shame which brings forth not sin but the glory of God, as Scripture says: "There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory" (Ecclus. 4:25). Cleanse your neck, so that your hair does not carry golden nets, nor [your neck] hanging necklaces, but rather wears those ornaments of which Scripture says: "Let mercy and faith not fail you, but hang them on your heart as on your neck" (Prov. 3:3). Cleanse your eyes, by drawing them back from all desire, never turning them away from the sight of the poor, and keeping them free of all paints in the sincerity in which they were made by God. Cleanse your tongue of lying, for "the mouth that lies kills the soul" (Wis. 1:11). Cleanse it of disparagement, of swearing, of flattery, of perjury. Do not think the order reversed because I said the tongue ought to be cleansed of swearing before perjury: for you will more easily escape perjury if you do not swear at all. Let that saying be fulfilled in you: "Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit" (Ps. 33:14). And remember the Apostle when he says: "Bless, and do not curse" (Rom. 12:14). But recall this more often: "See that no one repays anyone evil for good, nor curse for curse, but on the contrary blessing, for to this you have been called, that you may possess blessing as an inheritance" (1 Pet. 3:9); and this: "If anyone does not offend in speech, he is perfect" (Jas. 3:2). For it is wicked that those lips with which you confess, entreat, bless and praise the Lord should be polluted by the filth of any sin. I do not know with what conscience and with what tongue anyone entreats God with the tongue with which he either lies, or curses, or disparages. God hears holy lips, and quickly grants the prayers which a spotless tongue utters. Cleanse your ears, so that they give hearing only to holy and true words, so that they never take in obscene, or shameful, or worldly words, or hear anyone disparaging another, because of what is written: "Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not hear a wicked tongue" (Ecclus. 28:28); so that you may have a share with him of whom it is said that he was just in hearing and in sight, that is, he sinned neither with his ears nor with his eyes. Let your hands not be stretched out to receive, but drawn back from giving; not ready to strike, but very prompt for all works of mercy and compassion. Cleanse your feet, so that they do not go along the broad and spacious way which leads to the splendid and costly banquets of the world, but rather walk the steep and narrow road that leads to heaven, for it is written: "Make a straight path for your feet" (Isa. 57:14). Recognise that your members were formed by God the craftsman not for vices but for virtue; and when you have cleansed all your limbs of all filth of sin and have been sanctified in your whole body, then understand that your chastity will profit you, and await the palm of virginity with all confidence.

10. What it is to be holy in body I think I have set out briefly, indeed, but fully. Now we ought to learn what follows, "and in spirit": that is, that what it is wrong to do in deed, it should not be right to conceive in thought either. For she is holy as much in body as in spirit who sins neither in mind nor in heart, knowing also that God is the inspector of the heart; and therefore she takes pains to keep her soul, too, together with her body, clean from sin in every way, knowing that it is written: "Keep your heart with all watchfulness" (Prov. 4:23); and again: "The Lord loves holy hearts, and all the spotless are acceptable to him"; and elsewhere: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt. 5:8). This I think is said of those whom conscience convicts of no fault of sin. Of them, I believe, John said in his Epistle: "If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him" (1 John 3:20). I do not want you to think that you have escaped the charge of sin if the deed does not follow the will, since it is written: "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart" (Matt. 5:17). Nor should you say, "I thought of it, indeed, but did not carry it out": for even to desire is wrong. Hence blessed Peter commanded, saying: "Making your souls chaste" (1 Pet. 1:22); if he had known of no defilement of the soul, he would not have wished it to be made chaste. But we ought also to consider more attentively and observe that passage which contains: "These are they who have not defiled themselves with women, for they remained virgins: these follow the Lamb wherever he goes" (Rev. 14:4), [to see] whether they are joined to that divine company and range through all the storeys of the heavens by the merit of the integrity of chastity alone, or whether there are other things too, joined to which virginity attains the glory of so great a blessedness. But how shall we be able to know this? From what follows, unless I am mistaken, where it is written: "These were bought from among men as first-fruits for God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found: for they are without spot" (ibid. 14:5). You see, then, that they are not said to cling to the Lord's footsteps on account of one member only, but [that it is] those who besides virginity have led a life spotless from every contagion of sin. For this reason above all the virgin spurns marriage: that, being more free from care, she may more easily guard herself from every offence — which is required even of those who marry — and fulfil all the commandments of the law. For if she does not marry and nevertheless does the things from which even married women are commanded to be free, what will it profit [her] not to have married? For although no Christian is permitted to sin, and it is fitting that all who are cleansed by the sanctification of the spiritual washing should run their course in a spotless life, so that they may be taken into the inmost heart of the Church, which is described as being without spot, without wrinkle, without anything of the kind, yet it is much more necessary for the virgin to fulfil this, whom no husband, no children, no other necessity hinders from carrying out divine Scripture; nor will she be able to defend herself with any excuse if she sins.

11. O virgin, keep the resolve that is destined for you with a great reward. Glorious before God is the virtue of virginity and chastity, if it is not weakened by other lapses into sins and evils. Recognise your state, recognise your place, recognise your resolve. You are called the bride of Christ; see that you commit nothing unworthy of him to whom you are seen to be betrothed: he will quickly write a bill of divorce if he sees in you even one adultery. For any woman who is pledged with the tokens of a human betrothal at once anxiously and carefully asks the bridegroom's household, his intimates, his friends, and even his servants what character the young man has, what he loves most, what he accepts, how he lives, by what habits he governs himself, what dishes he eats, in what things he chiefly delights and rejoices. When she has learned these things, she so adjusts herself in all things that her compliance, her pleasantness, her diligence, her life agree with the bridegroom's character. You too, who have Christ as bridegroom, ask his household and intimates about the character of your bridegroom, and inquire vigorously and skilfully in what he chiefly delights, what arrangement of clothing he loves in you, what kind of adornment he desires. Let Peter, his closest intimate, tell you — who does not permit bodily adornment even to married women, as he wrote in his epistle: "Likewise, women, be subject to your husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of the women, observing in the fear of God your chaste conduct; let yours not be the outward [adornment] of hair, or the wearing of gold, or the finery of clothing, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God" (1 Pet. 3:1 ff.). Let another apostle, blessed Paul, also tell [you], who, writing to the bishop Timothy, testifies to the same thing concerning the discipline of faithful women: "Likewise, women, adorning themselves in seemly dress with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but as befits women professing chastity through good conduct" (1 Tim. 2:9).

12. But perhaps you say: why did the same apostles not command these things to virgins? Because they did not judge it necessary, lest such an admonition should seem to virgins an insult rather than a correction. Nor would they ever have believed that they would be so rash as to presume to take fleshly and earthly ornaments not granted even to married women. Truly a virgin ought to adorn and arrange herself; for how can she please her bridegroom unless she comes forth arranged and adorned? Let her be adorned, certainly, but with inner ornaments, and let her be arranged spiritually, not carnally, for God regards in her the beauty not of the body but of the soul. So you too, whoever desire your soul to be loved and indwelt by God, arrange it with all diligence and adorn it with spiritual garments. Let nothing unseemly, nothing foul appear in it. Let it shine with the gold of justice, gleam with the gems of holiness, and flash with the most precious pearl of chastity. Instead of fine linen and silk, let it be clothed with the tunic of mercy and compassion, according to what is written: "Put on, then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, heartfelt mercy, kindness, humility, etc." (Col. 3:12). And let it not seek the beauty of white lead or any other paint, but have the whiteness of innocence and simplicity. Let it possess the rosy colour of modesty and the crimson of blushing and shame. Let it be washed with the heavenly soda of doctrine and cleansed with spiritual laments. Let no stain of malice, no stain of the devil be left in it; and lest it ever smell foul with the odour of sin, let it be drenched with the ointment of the sweetest wisdom and knowledge.

13. Such adornment God seeks, and a soul so arranged he desires. Remember that you are called a daughter of God, according to what he says: "Hear, daughter, and see" (Ps. 44:11). And you yourself, whenever you name God as Father, testify that you are a daughter of God. So if you are a daughter of God, see that you do none of the things that are unbefitting to God the Father, but do everything as a daughter of God. Consider how the daughters of the nobles of this world conduct themselves, to what manners they accustom themselves, by what disciplines they train themselves. Some have such modesty, such gravity, such restraint that they surpass the ways of other people out of regard for their human high birth; and lest they brand their honourable parents with any mark of disgrace through a fall of their own, they strive to make for themselves among men, as it were, a second nature of habit. You too, then, look to your origin, consider your lineage, attend to the glory of your nobility: recognise that you are the daughter not of a man but of God, and adorned with the nobility of a divine birth. Show yourself such that the heavenly birth may appear in you and divine high birth shine out. Let there be in you a new gravity, an admirable honesty, an astonishing modesty, a wonderful patience, a virginal gait, the bearing of true chastity, and speech always modest and uttered in its proper time; so that whoever sees you may marvel and say: "What is this patience of a gravity new among men? What modesty of shame? What restraint of honesty? What ripeness of wisdom? Human training is not like this, nor mortal discipline: something heavenly breathes to me from this earthly body. I think that God dwells in certain people." And when he learns that you are Christ's handmaid, he will be held by greater astonishment and will consider what kind of Lord he is whose handmaid is such.

14. If, then, you wish to be with Christ and to have a share with Christ, you must live by the example of Christ, who was so estranged from all malice and wickedness that he did not repay even his enemies, but rather prayed for them. For I do not want you to consider those souls Christian which — I do not say hate their brothers or sisters — but do not love their neighbours with all their heart and conscience before the witness of God; since it is necessary for Christians, in the likeness of Christ, to love even their enemies. If you desire to have the fellowship of the saints, cleanse your breast of the thought of malice and wickedness. Let no one circumvent you, let no one lead you astray with deceitful speech. The heavenly court will receive none but the holy and just and simple and innocent and pure. Malice has no place with God. Whoever desires to reign with Christ must be clean of all wickedness and guile. Nothing is so contrary, nothing so execrable to God, as to hate anyone, to wish to harm anyone; nothing so commendable as to love all. Knowing this, the Prophet testifies, saying: "You who love the Lord, hate evil" (Ps. 96:10).

15. See that you do not love human glory in anything; lest your portion too be counted among those to whom it was said: "How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?" (John 5:44). And of whom it is said through the Prophet: "Increase evils for them, increase evils for the glorious of the earth." And elsewhere: "Be confounded at your glorying, at the reproach in the sight of God" (Isa. 45). For I do not want you to look to those who are virgins of the world, not of Christ; who, forgetful of their resolve and profession, rejoice in luxuries, delight in riches, and delight in the origin of bodily nobility. If they truly believed themselves to be daughters of God, they would never, after a divine birth, admire human nobility, nor glory in some honoured father: if they felt that they had God as Father, they would not love nobility of the flesh. Why do you flatter yourself and take pleasure in nobility of lineage? God made two human beings at the beginning, from whom the whole forest of the human race descends: worldly nobility was conferred not by the fairness of nature but by the ambition of greed. Certainly we are all made equal through the generation of the divine washing, and there can be no distinction among those whom the second birth has begotten; through which rich as well as poor, free as well as slave, noble as well as base-born, is made a son of God; and earthly nobility is overshadowed by the splendour of heavenly glory and no longer appears anywhere at all, while those who formerly were unequal in worldly honours are equally clothed with the glory of heavenly and divine nobility. There is no longer any place for low birth, nor is anyone degenerate whom the sublimity of divine birth adorns, except among those who do not think heavenly things are to be preferred to human ones: or, if they do think so, how vain it is that they should set themselves above, in lesser things, those whom they know to be their equals in greater things, and should reckon as placed beneath them on earth those whom they believe to be their equals in heaven! But you, whoever are a virgin of Christ and not of the world, flee all the glory of the present life, so that you may attain that which is promised in the future.

16. Avoid words of contention and causes of animosity; shun also occasions of discord and quarrels. For if, according to the Apostle's teaching, "the servant of the Lord must not quarrel" (2 Tim. 2:24), how much more the handmaid of God? Her mind ought to be the more restrained as her sex is the more modest. Restrain your tongue from evil-speaking, and put the bridle of the Law on your mouth; so that when you do speak, perhaps when to keep silent would be a sin, you take care not to say anything that would incur reproach. A word uttered is a stone thrown; therefore it must be thought over long before it is uttered. Blessed indeed are the lips that never let out what they would wish to call back again. The speech of a chaste mind ought also to be chaste, always building up its hearers rather than ever tearing them down, according to what the Apostle commanded, saying: "Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but whatever is good for the building up of faith, that it may give grace to the hearers" (Eph. 4:29). Precious to God is the tongue that knows not how to put words together apart from divine things; and holy is the mouth from which heavenly utterances are always brought forth. Deter detractors of the absent as malicious, by the authority of Scripture: for the Prophet records this among the virtues of the perfect man, if before the sight of the just the malicious man is brought to nothing who has uttered unwarranted things against his neighbour. It is not permitted to you to listen patiently to the disparagement of another; for you do not wish yours to be received by others (Ps. 74:5). For whatever goes against the Gospel of Christ is unjust, if you allow to be inflicted on another what you find grievous to have done to you by another. Accustom your tongue always to speak of good things, and attune your hearing rather to the praise of the good than to the disparagement of the wicked. See that whatever good you do, you do for God's sake; knowing that you will receive from the Lord reward only for what you have accomplished for the sake of fear and love of him. Strive to be holy rather than to seem so: for it profits nothing to be thought what one is not; and it is the guilt of a double sin, not to have what one is believed to have, and to feign what one does not have.

17. Delight in fasts rather than in feasts, mindful of that widow who did not depart from the temple, serving God with fasts and supplications day and night. And if a widow in Judaea was such, what kind of virgin of Christ is it fitting to be now? Love rather the banquet of divine reading, and long to be filled with spiritual dishes; and seek rather those foods by which the soul rather than the body is refreshed. Flee kinds of meat and wine as kindlings of heat and incitements of lust, and then use a little wine, if at all, when pain of the stomach and excessive bodily weakness compel. Conquer anger; restrain animosity; and whatever it is that brings repentance after the deed, shun it as the abomination of a crime close at hand. Quite tranquil and quiet, and estranged from all disturbance of rage, must be the mind that desires to be God's dwelling; who testifies through the Prophet and says: "Upon whom shall I rest, but upon the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?" (Isa. 66:2). Believe God to be the watcher of all your works and thoughts, and take care neither to do nor to think anything unworthy of the divine eyes.

18. When you wish to offer prayer, present yourself as one about to speak with the Lord. When you say a psalm, recognise whose words you are saying; and delight in compunction of mind rather than in the sweetness of a ringing voice. For God approves the tears of one singing psalms more than the charm of the voice, as the Prophet says: "Serve the Lord in fear, and exult to him with fear" (Ps. 2:11). Where there is fear and trembling, there is no raising of the voice, but the tearful and weeping lowliness of the soul. Apply diligence to all your actions, for it is written: "Cursed is the man who does the work of the Lord negligently" (Jer. 48:10). Let grace grow in you with the years, let justice grow with age; and let your faith appear the more perfect the older you are: for our Lord Jesus, who left us an example of living, advanced not only in bodily age but also in wisdom and spiritual grace before God and men (Luke 2:52). Any time in which you have not felt yourself better, I reckon you have lost. Keep the resolve of virginity you have begun to the very end; for virtue lies not in having begun only but in having completed, as the Lord says in the Gospel: "Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved" (Matt. 10:22). Take care not to give anyone even an occasion for desire: for your bridegroom God is jealous; for an adulteress against Christ is more criminal than one against a husband. Hence the Roman Church, animated without doubt by the apostolic spirit of him whose see it holds, has fittingly laid down recently so severe a sentence in such cases that it would scarcely judge worthy even of penance a woman who had violated a body sanctified to God by lustful defilement.

19. Be, then, a pattern of living for all, be an example; go before in conduct those whom you outrun in the sanctification of chastity. Show yourself a virgin in all things; let no corruption be charged against your head, whose body is intact, so that your way of life too may be inviolable. And since, as we said at the beginning of the letter, you have been made a sacrifice of God, which indeed imparts its holiness to others as well, so that whoever worthily partakes of it becomes himself a sharer in sanctification; so then through you too, as through a divine victim, let the other women be sanctified, among whom you should so conduct yourself in all things that whoever comes into contact with your life, by hearing or by sight, may feel the power of sanctification, and may understand grace to be poured into him from your way of life to such a degree that, while he longs to imitate you, he too may become worthy of the sacrifice of God.
